title: Conjugate updating
dek: A conjugate prior is one that stays in the same family after multiplication by the likelihood. It is a computational convenience, not a moral law.
story: If p(θ) and f(y|θ) multiply to a kernel in the same family as p(θ), you can update by arithmetic. Beta–Binomial, Gamma–Poisson, Normal–Normal (known variance) are the three you will actually use on a whiteboard.

The update has a story: Beta(a,b) plus y successes in n trials becomes Beta(a+y, b+n−y). The prior acted like a−1 extra successes and b−1 extra failures in the Uniform-as-Beta(1,1) counting, or like a pseudo-counts of a and b in the mean a/(a+b) counting — say which convention you are using.
Most GLMs, mixed models, and phylogenetic models are not conjugate. Then conjugacy is a building block inside a Gibbs sampler or a variational factor, not the whole posterior.
deep: Poisson(λ) with Gamma(α, β) rate prior (shape-rate): posterior Gamma(α + ∑ yᵢ, β + n). Mean (α + ∑ y)/(β + n) shrinks ȳ toward α/β. This is empirical-Bayes cousin to a random-effect Poisson.
Normal mean, known σ², prior N(μ₀, τ₀²): posterior precision 1/τₙ² = 1/τ₀² + n/σ², posterior mean a precision-weighted average of μ₀ and ȳ. That one line is hierarchical shrinkage in a tuxedo.
Dirichlet–multinomial is the compositional version for lineage frequencies. Pseudo-counts stop you from writing log 0 when a lineage is unseen in a small district.
Conjugacy does not calibrate you. A conjugate posterior can be overconfident if the likelihood was iid fiction. Posterior predictive checks still apply.

formulas.label: Beta–Binomial
formulas.expression: π ~ Beta(a,b),  y|π ~ Bin(n,π)  ⇒  π|y ~ Beta(a+y, b+n−y)

formulas.label: Gamma–Poisson (shape-rate)
formulas.expression: λ ~ G(α,β),  yᵢ iid Pois(λ)  ⇒  λ|y ~ G(α+∑y, β+n)
formulas.note: Rate β; mean α/β. Check your software’s shape-scale convention.

visual.caption: Conjugate arithmetic: prior counts plus data counts, same family. The plate is a bookkeeping diagram, not a claim that the world is Beta.

example.title: Gamma–Poisson for a quiet week of cases
example.setup: Prior for a district weekly rate λ: Gamma(shape 2, rate 1/2), mean 4. Observe y = 0 this week. Update.

steps.title: Posterior
steps.body: Gamma(2+0, 0.5+1) = Gamma(2, 1.5). Mean 2/1.5 ≈ 1.33. The zero pulled the mean down; the prior stopped you at 0.

steps.title: Predictive
steps.body: A new week still has a chance of 0, 1, 2… under the posterior predictive (Negative binomial in this conjugate pair). Do not quote λ̂ = 0 as the district’s rate.

steps.title: If y = 20
steps.body: Gamma(22, 1.5), mean ≈ 14.7, closer to the data. Conjugacy is shrinkage that knows n.

example.takeaway: Pseudo-counts are the prior. Arithmetic is the posterior. Calibration is a separate question.

choices: The posterior stays in the same parametric family as the prior after multiplying by the likelihood
The MLE equals the posterior mean always
check.answer: The posterior stays in the same parametric family as the prior after multiplying by the likelihood
check.why: A kernel-closed update. Truth and equality with the MLE are extra.

whyWrong.MCMC is forbidden: Gibbs often uses conjugacy inside MCMC.
whyWrong.The MLE equals the posterior mean always: Only in limits or special priors.

check.prompt: π ~ Beta(4,4), then y = 0 successes in n = 2 trials. Posterior mean is:
check.why: Posterior Beta(4+0, 4+2) = Beta(4,6). Mean 4/10 = 0.4. The prior mean 0.5 was pulled toward the two failures.

whyWrong.0.5: That is the prior mean, pre-data.
whyWrong.0: The MLE is 0; the conjugate mean is not.
whyWrong.0.25: That would be 2/8 or a different pseudo-count mix.

check.prompt: On the conjugate flow plate, the last node “posterior predictive” is fed by the posterior, not by the prior alone. That means:
check.figureHint: Arrow from Beta(a+y, b+n−y) down to posterior predictive.
choices: New data are scored under p(ỹ | y), which integrates the updated θ, not under the original prior predictive
The posterior predictive is the likelihood L(θ|y)
The prior is discarded before predicting
check.answer: New data are scored under p(ỹ | y), which integrates the updated θ, not under the original prior predictive
check.why: Bookkeeping continues after the update. Calibration later uses these predictives.

whyWrong.The posterior predictive is the likeliho: Different object: L is a curve in θ; a posterior predictive is a distribution on ỹ.
whyWrong.Conjugacy forbids prediction: The opposite — it makes p(ỹ|y) easy (Beta-Binomial, NB, …).
whyWrong.The prior is discarded before predicting: It is already inside the posterior.
